Some things to note, which you didn't ask for, but I am providing anyway. I believe everyone should learn to write and communicate more effectively. I always want to learn and improve. If you do not want constructive criticism, stop reading.

  • Your paper should never change font, color, or size throughout the paper unless for literary effect.
  • You should not quote BMI definitions from a paper as it is a secondary source and should have gone with the primary source. In this case reference the governing health body, WHO definitions or quote who they use for definitions.
  • Work on your flow introducing quotes and sources. There is a choppiness to it that breaks the readers train of thought
  • You should refrain from using first-person, unless this was a requirement for the paper (a personal reflection, journal etc.). This skews your message towards your bias. While you are trying to convey a point, it is combined with an innate skew that weakens the overall power of the paper.
  • Watch your sentence flow and word choice. "America literally consumes twice as much food than is typically needed". You repeated the same idea you presented in the previous sentence, which disrespects the reader ("You can't figure out it is double, I'll say it again"). The world "literally" is not necessary and this unnecessary word use frequently occurs (repetition can be a helpful tool if used sparingly).
  • A period is outside of the quote at a sentence end. "quote text, text". You do not have to quote the full sentence.
  • Try to avoid secondary sources (USA today - they are referencing someone, which will be a great resource). You are referencing someone, who is referencing someone. If you quoted the USA Today's author's words that would be fine.
  • Don't be afraid to break up a quote - "More than half — 56% — of U.S. adults were...". That is the paper's writing style. You can quote the CDC study and say 56%.
  • Make sure to introduce an acronym/initialism first to use the short form. In the line referenced above your quote uses CDC, which is not defined, and in the next sentence you quote "Centers for Disease Control". You can truncate the quote to capture the fact and avoid the unnecessary words (although it does boost your word count :) )
  • Practice word choice, you are quoting this: "That fuel spewed an estimated 3.8 million extra tons of carbon dioxide into the air". Spewed works, but you can paraphrase and present the fact in your style: "An extra 3.8 million tons, were released..." or "The high-carbon atmosphere was burdened with an unnecessary 3.8 million tons of CO2, the equivalent of X, due to obese passengers' excess weight".
  • The paper as whole seems like your text is gluing quotes together. A paper needs to do this, but your collection of the quotes needs to be greater than the sum of its parts. A paper is "here is my thesis and how I support it", not "these quotes fit my world view". Similar ideas, but very distinct concepts. Ask yourself: What value does the reader gain by reviewing my work?
  • The over-arching flow of the paper is lost by the end. You state at the beginning that social harm for obesity is "complex", yet imply you remove all complexity in two pages. It would have been stronger and easier to write under the thesis that the obesity crisis is causing social harm. Have a section on points defending the idea, a section on refuting their beliefs and a section on refuting their attacks against your points.

Of course not; you simply hide your bias. Absolute nonsense, unless you're interested in rhetoric over substance. Many journals are belatedly recognizing this.

Not to be more objective, but to hinder yourself from not completing a point and to promote reader discovery and help a writer develop skills. By removing yourself from your writings it requires you to fill it in with extra detail; not that it cannot be done in first-person, but for someone developing writing technique, it forces a coherent argument. They are finding points that fit their argument, but they do not get luxury of writing in that manner, they must rework the material to a different perspective. Additional working memory time leads to additional learning and proficiency.

With reader discovery you can present your argument and the facts, but it is not personalized to you. The reader can internally discover if they agree with the argument and can question the authors true intentions. Any biases the reader holds of the writer are hidden. I'm making these conclusions based of X rather than I think Y because of X; a bottom up-approach rather than top-down. This is more stylistic than anything.

I would argue for upcoming writers, forcing themselves to write about an argument from a different perspective is beneficial to the learning process.

(I would also say journals are transition to an active rather than passive voice over third to first. I don't think I have ever read a methods section written in first (or second) person, not that it can't be done. I would be very surprised if this switch is occurring, it seems incongruent to the ideals of science [from a human bias perspective, not objectively].
